newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INTERVIEW-North sees costs as key.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-North sees costs as key.

text.p: By James Regan,

Diversified resources group North Ltd said on Wednesday that having its eggs in many baskets offers protection from cyclical commodities downturns but the real key to beating the market is to keep costs down.
"The key driver is to preferably be in the lower cost quartile, certainly in the lower half," North managing director Campbell Anderson told Reuters in an interview.
North mines uranium and gold at home, is digging for copper in Argentina and zinc in Sweden, and is the world's fourth largest producer of iron ore, from Western Australia and Canada.
North is also involved in forest products in Australia.
The company made a net profit of A$111.9 million for the year ended June 30, 1996 and the bottom line for the year just ended is looking a little better than that, Anderson said.

In nearly all its businesses, North is aiming to lift output, determined not to get caught producing small quantities of commodities when the inevitable price cycles for commodities heads down, he said.
Low points in gold and uranium are currently evident and it is only a matter of time before prices for other commodities turn, Anderson said.
One goal is to shore up as many customers as possible to ensure a high percentage of production finds a ready home.
Most of the Australian iron ore goes to Japanese steel mills while Canadian iron ore goes to the big U.S. mills, he said.
Zinc is sold exclusively to Belgium's Union Miniere SA Industrial Group.
Sixty percent of the 5,000 tonnes or so of uranium produced is pre-purchased by utilities in Japan and elsewhere.
Even copper from North's 25 percent owned Alumbrera Mine in the foothills of the Andes in Argentina is pre-sold, even though it is not scheduled to start operating until later in 1997.
North views its commodities businesses as either "price takers" or "price makers," Anderson said.
International markets dictate the prices of most base and precious metals but in other products, North sees opportunities to realise price premiums, he said.
"We put in an enormous effort to ensure that we are a preferred supplier in our iron ore uranium and fibre businesses," Anderson said.
"You don't want to get hit with a double whammy of low market prices and low volumes," he said.
Under criticism from environmentalists in Australia for its uranium, gold and timber businesses, North hasn't ruled out expanding at home but also is looking overseas, Anderson said.

He said the US$230 million purchase of a 59.3 percent stake in Iron Ore Co of Canada last January hopefully would give North a boost in supplying ore to a growing number of smaller steel mills using electric arc furnaces as well as big steel mills.
A year earlier it bought Zinkgruvan in Sweden, a business Anderson said he would now like to see grow.
"Our preferred basis is the acquisition, either by purchase or by exploration, of a good mine ore body which we would then operate," Anderson said.

Through its listed subsidiary Energy Resources of Australia Ltd, North plans to develop additional uranium mines in order to capture what Anderson believes is growth in demand for the metal from the nuclear power generating industry.
This year, ERA will produce about 7.5 percent of the world market for uranium and, in future years, lift its share to about nine percent, Anderson said.
Plans to develop one of the largest gold mines in eastern Australia, knocked back once over environmental concerns may no longer make economic sense given depressed gold prices, he said.

North has already spent A$26 million on predevelopment of Lake Cowal gold project but production costs would probably exceed the current gold price, leaving North "in no rush" to bring the mine on stream, Anderson said.
Clearly the main focus now for North is on iron ore.
"Iron ore has been very significantly the largest part of our operation," Anderson said.
Beside its existing iron ore operations, North is spending A$20 million to assess the possibility of developing its West Angelas ore deposit in Western Australia in about 2000.
The mine would initially produces about 10 million tonnes of ore a year eventually building up to 20 million tonnes.
